explanations.answer: That he won't need to be as bold as he expects
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul writes, "I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh." (2 Corinthians 10:2) He's hoping for a gentle visit. I think he'd much rather show up and share cookies than give a lecture.

explanations.answer: That they'll have the whole church gathered
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about a gathering here. What he begs for is that he won't need to be as bold as he expects when he comes (2 Corinthians 10:2). I think he'd rather have a quiet visit. A big meeting sounds like a lot of folding chairs.

explanations.answer: That they'll find him a place to stay
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but Paul isn't asking for a room. He begs that he "may not need to be as bold as I expect" when he comes (2 Corinthians 10:2). His request is about how the visit goes, not where he sleeps. Nobody's fluffing pillows in this verse.

Careful, friend. Paul says the opposite: "The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh." (2 Corinthians 10:4) He says they live in the flesh but don't wage war according to the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:3). So the weapons are of another kind.

That's right, friend. Paul says, "The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh." (2 Corinthians 10:4) Then he tells us what they are instead: weapons with divine power. He's not swinging a rolling pin here.
Yes, friend. Paul says these weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds." (2 Corinthians 10:4) The power isn't from us. It comes from God, and that's why the weapons work.
Fancy word, friend, but it's not Paul's. He says the weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds." (2 Corinthians 10:4) No crowns or thrones are mentioned. The power is divine.

I see why you'd pick it, since Paul does talk about warfare. But he says these weapons are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, "they have divine power to demolish strongholds." (2 Corinthians 10:4) So the power isn't military. It's divine.

explanations.answer: To make it obedient to Christ
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul says, "we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) The point isn't winning. It's obedience to Christ. Even my wandering thoughts about the cookie jar need to hear that.

Paul doesn't mention enemies in this verse. He says we take captive every thought "to make it obedient to Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) The thoughts are the target, and Christ is the goal. Nobody's getting hushed.

explanations.answer: To win every debate in town
explanations.explanation: Sounds like a fun trophy, friend, but that's not in the verse. Paul says we take every thought captive "to make it obedient to Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) The goal is obedience to Christ, not debate wins. Nobody's keeping score at the town hall.

Yes, friend. Paul says they'll be ready to punish disobedience "as soon as your obedience is complete." (2 Corinthians 10:6) So the Corinthians' own obedience comes first. Their obedience is what he's waiting on.

Titus was Paul's coworker, and he does come up elsewhere in this letter (2 Corinthians 7:6). But here Paul says nothing about a report. He says, "as soon as your obedience is complete." (2 Corinthians 10:6) What has to be complete is the Corinthians' obedience.

Paul does write about a collection for the saints in this letter (2 Corinthians 9:1). But that's not what he's waiting on here. He says, "as soon as your obedience is complete." (2 Corinthians 10:6) It's their obedience that has to be complete.

That's right, friend. Paul says anyone confident that he belongs to Christ "should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does." (2 Corinthians 10:7) Nobody gets to claim Christ all to themselves. Paul belongs to Him too.

Not this time, friend. Paul really does say it: "If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does." (2 Corinthians 10:7) So the statement is true. Paul belongs to Christ just as much as anyone.
Close, friend, but Paul says the reverse. The authority the Lord gave is "for building you up rather than tearing you down." (2 Corinthians 10:8) So it's for building up, not tearing down.

That's right, friend. Paul says the Lord gave him authority "for building you up rather than tearing you down." (2 Corinthians 10:8) It's for building up, not tearing down. Think of a good baker's helper who adds to the batch instead of knocking over the cooling rack.

Yes, friend. Some say, "His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account." (2 Corinthians 10:10) Ouch. That's quite a review. I know a little about being called unimpressive, back when I was a stamper in a drawer.

That's the opposite, friend. The critics say his letters are "weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive." (2 Corinthians 10:10) So they say his letters are the strong part. In person, they say, he doesn't impress.

Good guess, but that's not the word. The critics say his "physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account." (2 Corinthians 10:10) They're saying he doesn't impress, not that he's unwelcome.

explanations.answer: In person the actions will match the letters
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul says, "what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present." (2 Corinthians 10:11) His words on paper and his actions in person will line up. What you read is what you get.

explanations.answer: Someone else wrote all of the letters
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything like that. He says that "what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present." (2 Corinthians 10:11) The letters are his, and his actions will match them.

explanations.answer: No more letters are coming to them
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He tells the critics to consider that "what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present." (2 Corinthians 10:11) It's about his actions matching his letters, not about how many letters are left.

Yes, friend. Paul says, "When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance." (2 Corinthians 10:12) Grading yourself against yourself tells you nothing. The ruler has to come from somewhere else.

Humble people don't usually hand themselves a trophy, friend. Paul says that when they measure themselves by themselves, "they show their ignorance." (2 Corinthians 10:12) The word is ignorance, not humility.

Not quite, friend. Paul says that when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, "they show their ignorance." (2 Corinthians 10:12) The word is ignorance, not wisdom.

That's right, friend. Paul says he'll boast only "within the field of influence that God has assigned to us—a field that reaches even to you." (2 Corinthians 10:13) The Corinthians are inside that field. Paul isn't reaching into someone else's yard.
Not this time, friend. Paul says God assigned a field "that reaches even to you." (2 Corinthians 10:13) The "you" is the Corinthians. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: The gospel first reached them through Paul
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, "we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:14) Since he got there first, he isn't overstepping. That's his reason, straight from the text.

explanations.answer: The other apostles gave Corinth to Paul
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that here. His reason is, "we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:14) He got there first, and nobody handed anything over.

explanations.answer: Paul was born and raised in Corinth
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says, friend. Paul's reason is, "we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:14) It's about bringing the gospel first, not about where he grew up.

That's it, friend. Paul writes, "we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well." (2 Corinthians 10:15) Their faith grows, and so does his reach among them.

explanations.answer: The size of their gifts to Paul
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about gifts to him here. He hopes that "as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well." (2 Corinthians 10:15) What grows is his influence.

Good try, friend, but Paul doesn't mention teachers. He hopes that "as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well." (2 Corinthians 10:15) It's his influence that grows.

explanations.answer: So he can preach in the regions beyond them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul hopes his influence grows "so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you." (2 Corinthians 10:16) He wants to keep going and reach new places. Corinth isn't the finish line.

explanations.answer: So he can settle down in Corinth for good
explanations.explanation: Paul's looking the other way, friend. He wants to "preach the gospel in the regions beyond you." (2 Corinthians 10:16) That means moving on to new places, not settling down.

explanations.answer: So he can lead every church in all of Greece
explanations.explanation: That's a big job, friend, and Paul doesn't claim it. He says he wants to "preach the gospel in the regions beyond you." (2 Corinthians 10:16) It's about preaching in new places, not leading every church.
Yes, friend. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (2 Corinthians 10:17) He's quoting Jeremiah, a prophet of Israel. If there's a boast to be made, it goes to the Lord.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (2 Corinthians 10:17) The Lord is the one to boast in, not the law.
I see why you'd think of it, since the temple was a big deal. But Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (2 Corinthians 10:17) The boast goes to the Lord, not a building.

Careful, friend. Paul says it the other way around: "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends." (2 Corinthians 10:18) Praising yourself doesn't get you approved.

That's right, friend. Paul says, "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends." (2 Corinthians 10:18) Self-praise doesn't count. The Lord's approval does.
